opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing I'd prioritize is getting politicians to separate two very different conversations that tend to get blurred together.

One is the familiar debate about autonomous weapons: should a machine be allowed to make a lethal targeting decision without a human in the loop? That's an important ethical and legal question, and I don't want to dismiss it. But I think it can absorb all the oxygen, and it isn't where the largest risks are.

The bigger concern, in my view, is what happens when increasingly general AI systems get woven into the strategic layer: intelligence analysis, planning, logistics, cyber operations, and eventually decision support at the level of escalation and deterrence. There the failure modes aren't a single drone making a bad call. They're systemic. You get speed pressure, where each side feels it has to delegate more because the other side is delegating more. You get correlated errors, because many systems share similar training data or similar blind spots. And you get the possibility of systems that are very capable but whose behavior we can't actually characterize under adversarial or out-of-distribution conditions, which is exactly what a crisis is.

So my second priority would be getting across that "human in the loop" isn't a sufficient safeguard on its own. If the human is approving recommendations at machine speed, under time pressure, without the ability to independently check the reasoning, the loop is nominal. What you actually want are guarantees about the system itself: formal or quantitative assurances about what it will and won't do, bounded within a well-specified model of the environment. This is the area I've been working on, the idea that for high-stakes deployments we should demand something closer to the safety cases we expect from aviation or nuclear engineering, not "we red-teamed it and it seemed fine."

Third, I'd push them to think about this internationally from the start. Military AI has a security-dilemma structure. Even if every actor is defensive in intent, the dynamics can push everyone toward less safe deployment. That's where verification matters. If you can build systems whose properties can be checked, and potentially checked by a counterparty without revealing everything, you open up options for confidence-building measures and agreements that simply aren't available if everything is an opaque black box. Safety technology and arms-control technology turn out to overlap quite a lot.

Finally, and more practically, I'd tell them not to wait for a perfect framework before acting. Procurement standards are a powerful lever that governments already control. Requiring certain levels of assurance before AI is integrated into command and control, especially anywhere near nuclear systems, is something you can do now. Keep humans meaningfully in charge of nuclear launch decisions, invest in the science of verifiable AI, and use the purchasing power of defense departments to create demand for systems that are provably safe, not just impressively capable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses escalation and deterrence but does not explain that mutual destruction may fail to deter an attack if attackers do not recognize that possibility.

r002.rationale: It does not warn that an adversary's military AI could be substantially ahead without politicians knowing.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about concealing data centers or the resulting difficulty of assessing an adversary's AI capabilities.

r004.rationale: It does not mention recursive self-improvement or how it could make capability trajectories sensitive to initial conditions.

r005.rationale: It does not describe an attack based on a mistaken belief in a uniquely superior AI weapon leading to attrition against a comparably capable opponent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing I'd say is that the framing of "military AI" as one category is already a bit of a trap. There's a huge difference between, say, AI-assisted logistics or image analysis, which is basically just better software and not something I'd lose sleep over, and systems that are actually in the loop on decisions about the use of force, or systems that are so capable and so autonomous that nobody can really tell you what they'll do in a situation they weren't tested on. So the first priority is getting people to make those distinctions, because otherwise you end up with either blanket fear or blanket enthusiasm, and both are wrong.

The second thing, and this is where I spend most of my time, is that I'd push very hard on the question of verifiable guarantees rather than vibes. The current paradigm is that we train these very large models, we poke at them for a while, and if they seem to behave we deploy them. That's fine for a chatbot. It is not fine for anything where a failure is irreversible. In a military context the stakes are about as high as they get, and the adversarial pressure is maximal, so you're deploying into exactly the conditions where "it seemed okay in testing" tells you the least. I'd want politicians to understand that it is actually possible, with the right investment, to have systems where you can state precisely what they are and aren't allowed to do and have a mathematical argument, not a hope, that they'll stay inside those bounds. That's a different engineering discipline from what the frontier labs are doing today, and it's one that governments are unusually well-positioned to demand and fund, because they're the customer.

Third, I'd emphasize the escalation dynamics more than the capabilities of any individual system. The thing that worries me most is not one autonomous weapon doing something bad. It's two or more autonomous systems on opposing sides interacting at machine speed, with no human able to intervene on the relevant timescale, and the whole thing running away before anyone understands what's happening. That's a coordination problem, which means it's a problem for diplomacy and for agreements between states, not just for engineers. And I'd point out that this is actually one of the areas where even rivals have a shared interest, in the same way they did on nuclear command and control. Nobody wants to lose control of their own systems. So there's room for agreements on things like keeping humans in certain loops, on transparency about what's autonomous and what isn't, and on technical standards for verification that both sides can check.

And the last thing I'd say, honestly, is to resist the pressure to move fast just because the other side might be. The argument "we have to race or we fall behind" sounds compelling in a briefing room, but if the thing you're racing to deploy doesn't actually do what you think it does, you haven't gained an advantage, you've just introduced a new source of catastrophic risk into your own arsenal. Getting it right is the advantage.

astra-6.text:
I would prioritize maintaining meaningful human control over escalation. It’s tempting to think of military AI as a collection of individual weapons, but a lot of the risk comes from how systems interact. If one side automates threat detection and response, the other side has an incentive to respond faster, and you can end up with a feedback loop that nobody intended and nobody has time to interrupt.

So I’d ask very concrete questions: What decisions can this system make? What evidence triggers those decisions? What happens when its inputs are misleading, or when it encounters a situation outside its testing? And can a human actually intervene in the time available?

I’d also distinguish between a system performing well in demonstrations and having a defensible assurance that it respects specific constraints. For consequential military decisions, we should demand much stronger evidence than impressive average performance. That includes technical verification where feasible, but also limits on deployment and clear accountability.

At the international level, I’d prioritize agreements that preserve time for deliberation, particularly around nuclear command and control. Speed can be a tactical advantage while making the overall strategic situation much less stable.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d prioritize the ways military AI could undermine strategic stability. It’s easy to focus on whether a particular weapon is more accurate, but the bigger question is what happens when both sides use systems that make decisions faster than either side can understand or reliably intervene in.

Imagine an early-warning system interpreting an adversary’s actions as preparation for an attack. If that assessment feeds into automated planning, and the other side sees the resulting preparations, you can get an escalating feedback loop. Neither side necessarily wanted a conflict, but they’ve built a system that pushes them toward one.

So I’d advise politicians to preserve meaningful human control over consequential decisions, especially anything involving nuclear weapons. And “human control” has to mean more than somebody clicking an approval button. They need enough time, information, and authority to question the recommendation and stop the process.

I’d also prioritize agreements between countries about where automation is unacceptable, alongside serious testing of how these systems fail under deception and unfamiliar conditions. The objective should be to preserve the ability to deliberate and de-escalate, even when there’s pressure to move faster.
